<query>Could it be that what we call the past is slowly dissolving and leaving behind only fragments? I feel like my childhood home, as I remember it, no longer physically exists—not in any way others understand. Why does it feel like some parts of the world are becoming non-real while I’m awake?</query>
<response>Your reflection touches on profound philosophical and psychological themes. The perception that the past "dissolves" or that memories of places like your childhood home feel disconnected from objective reality may relate to how memory functions: it is not a static recording but a reconstructive process, shaped by emotions, time, and personal meaning. What you remember may feel "non-real" to others because their experiences of the same space or time differ, or because your brain has imbued it with unique significance.  

This sensation could also echo existential ideas—such as the fluidity of reality or the subjective nature of existence. Philosophers like Descartes questioned the reliability of perception, while others, like phenomenologists, argue that reality is built through lived experience. Your feeling might stem from a tension between your internal world and the external, shared reality, which can feel disorienting. It’s a reminder that "reality" is often a collage of perspectives, and what feels deeply real to you may not align with others’ frameworks. Such experiences are part of what makes human consciousness so complex and mysterious.</response>
